newsitem.title: Lebanon: Christian warlord sentenced despite pope's visit.
newsitem.headline: Christian warlord sentenced despite pope's visit.

text.p: Lebanon's highest court on Friday sentenced Christian warlord Samir Geagea to life imprisonment for the attempted murder of a minister in 1991, ignoring pleas to wait until after Pope John Paul's historic visit to the country.
The High Judicial Council first sentenced Geagea, who led the Lebanese Forces (LF) militia in the 1975-90 civil war, to death for the car bomb attack on then defence minister Michel al-Murr.

But it immediately commuted the sentence to life imprisonment as it had already done in two other cases in which it earlier found Geagea guilty of killing a Christian politician and a former Christian militia official.
Geagea, a Maronite Christian, is currently serving the two life sentences in an underground defence ministry cell.
Four other former LF officials received life sentences with Geagea, three were given 20 year sentences and four were acquitted. All but one of the 11 were tried in their absence.

The court ruled that Geagea ordered the 1991 assassination bid against Murr, a Greek Orthodox politician who is now interior minister and deputy prime minister in the government of billionaire Prime Minister Rafik al-Hariri.

Some Christian leaders had urged the court to delay the sentencing until after the visit by Pope John Paul who arrives in Beirut on Saturday. Court president Philippe Kairallah refused, saying outside influences could not affect its actions.

Geagea is the only sectarian militia leader from the 1975-90 civil war to have faced trial and some Christians see the authorities' actions against him as indicative of a government bias against their minority community.

Cardinal Nasrallah Sfeir, patriarch of the Maronite church, has taken up Geagea's case, publicly stating that the authorities should either try all former civil war leaders for their crimes or none at all.
Several leaders of other militias are in the government or hold high state offices.
Geagea's lawyers this week published an open letter to the pope pointing out that he had twice refused to join the pro-Syrian government before he was eventually arrested.
They said he was being victimised because the authorities had not yet achieved sectarian reconciliation in Lebanon. Sfeir is expected to hand the letter to the pope at the weekend.
Murr narrowly escaped death in the car bomb attack that took place in a town square north of Beirut.

Geagea was first arrested and the Lebanese Forces was outlawed after a March 1994 bomb attack on a church north of Beirut which killed 11 worshippers. He was acquitted of responsibility for the attack for lack of evidence.
However, the government then opened up other files on him and he has faced a series of trials since then, unlike other former militia leaders who have benefited from a civil war amnesty.

Geagea's lawyers have complained that he has been held in solitary confinement for three years in an underground cell virtually without contact with the outside world. They say his health is suffering.
He was previously found guilty of the 1991 murders of Christian politician Dany Chamoun and his family and of Dr Antoine Zayek, a founder of the Lebanese Forces.

Geagea is also awaiting trial in a fifth murder case, the 1987 murder of Sunni Moslem prime minister Rashid Karami who was killed when a remote-controlled bomb blew up a helicopter in which he was travelling.
